en: Compiled by Shi Dunlun, *Jizhuan lunben*, Fascicle 46.
From here on, the fifteenth section explains the four *udānas*. If the character is written as "嗢" (*wu*), it must all be corrected.
Correct. The old terminology was incorrect;
it is called the four udānas.
The term is translated as "seal" (mudrā),
but here it is translated as "discourse" (vyākaraṇa);
that is, what the World-Honored One constantly recites and expounds.
This meaning appears to be an unasked spontaneous teaching (*anupṛṣṭa-svavacana*).
Depending on the context, it may also be termed a "seal" (*mudrā*),
or "summary meaning" (*piṇḍārtha*), or "distinguishing mark" (*lakṣaṇa*).
As it is said: impermanence is the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena;
suffering is the defining characteristic of tainted phenomena;
and selflessness is the defining characteristic of all phenomena.
Nirvāṇa-śānti (the tranquility of nirvāṇa) is the defining characteristic of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If it is called *uḍḍāna*, then it is called "collective presentation" (*saṃgraha*);
because it is thus termed *uḍḍāna*, it is a defining characteristic.
In this text, first the number is raised and the names are listed;
second, the meaning of *udāna* is explained;
third, the explanation is provided in sequence according to four meanings.
The *udāna* is explained through three meanings.
Regarding the meaning of "concordance with the Dharma" (*dharmasaṃprayukta*),
it refers to the concordance of impermanence with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), and so forth.
Regarding "successively proclaiming":
as the Buddhas of the past taught these four dharmas which have been transmitted to the present,
so the Buddhas of the present teach these four dharmas which shall be transmitted to the future.
Ordinary beings who rely on these four modes of practice and are able to proceed toward the superior fruits of humans and devas are said to be "proceeding toward a great birth.
Noble ones who rely on these four modes of practice and attain liberation from the three realms are said to be "emerging into the foremost."
In the explanation of the initial meaning of impermanence, there is a question regarding the resolution of bondage.
Within this resolution, there are two parts:
first, the resolution of impermanence by way of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the thoroughly imagined nature).
The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states:
"The meaning of 'non-existence' is the meaning of 'impermanence,' because conceptualized characteristics (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) are ultimately non-existent.
Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Moreover, by observing that... onwards, the second [section] explains impermanence by means of the phenomena of dependent origination (*paratantra*).
Within this, there are three parts:
first, contemplating the impermanence of the dependent nature;
second, discerning impermanence by way of the three periods of time.
Third, distinguishing impermanence by means of the four characteristics (*caturlakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the initial statement, "Up to the point where arising and ceasing can be apprehended, with ignorance as their cause," Jing says:
This clarifies that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is inexpressible;
just as the eye perceives form,
so too, up to the body’s sensation of touch, it is inexpressible.
It is like drinking cold water;
the one who has realized it knows for themselves that verbal expression cannot adequately describe what was realized.
Such is the nature of the self-characteristics of all phenomena arising from causes and conditions.
If one wishes to speak by way of arising, one speaks only of the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*);
that is to say, when one speaks of "form" (*rūpa*) in general, it exhausts the essence of all forms,
and when one speaks of "blue," it exhausts all blue things.
Just as the eye-faculty perceives a single moment of form in a single thought-moment, so too its own-characteristic perishes at that very instant; thus it is said to be unobtainable.
Because its nature cannot be fully understood through words, one clings to a fixed nature according to those verbal expressions—this is the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
When grasped in this manner, the seeds perfumed thereby become the cause;
thus, those dependent phenomena such as form and mind arise and immediately perish,
and are therefore called impermanent.
Ce says: Because one does not understand the two kinds of reality, such as the "as-it-is-ness" (yathāvad-bhāvikatā), and the four kinds of worldly reality (loka-vitatha-samjñā),
various conceptual proliferations (prapañca) and the ignorance of clinging to phenomena (dharma-grāha) arise.
The arising and ceasing of the various mundane, outflow-tainted five aggregates can be observed.
Next, one contemplates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three times are impermanent.
Because those conditioned phenomena have no cause that can be found and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This clarifies that those past formations lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and also lack a productive cause.
Cè states: "Regarding this passage, there are two Western interpretations."
One explanation states:
According to the principles of the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the three periods of time are established within a single present dharma.
That is to say, because that which is present has not previously existed, it is termed "future."
That which does not exist is called "past";
that which has already existed but is not yet extinguished is called "present.
This is according to the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
If one relies on conventional reasoning,
it may also be said that the past and future exist,
because they have existed and will exist.
Based on this principle, one may say that things exist, do not exist, both exist and do not exist, or neither exist nor do not exist.
This refutation targets the position of those masters who maintain that the three dharmas across the three periods of time all possess substantial reality.
The second says:
The principle of *vijñapti-mātra* establishes the three periods of time;
that is to say, the appearances of the three periods manifest upon the substance of the present seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).
Therefore, the three time periods are spoken of;
yet in reality, they are subsumed within the present.
Question: Since the past and future are non-existent, how can they be impermanent?
The Tripitaka Master offers two interpretations.
The first states:
"In the future, things are originally non-existent; because they are destined to exist, they are called impermanent."
The past is also non-existent because it has already occurred; therefore, it is called impermanent.
The second interpretation states:
that which is to be named is the future.
Because that which is currently existing must eventually become non-existent, it is called impermanent.
Its returning to non-existence is called the past;
because that which was currently existing returns to non-existence, it is called the impermanence of the past.
In the third [section], the contemplation of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*): first, the four characteristics are distinguished;
second, the external attachments are extensively refuted.

Regarding the statement in the preceding section that "each and every moment possesses three characteristics, and following that moment, there is further a fourth characteristic of the conditioned," Jing says:
"The three characteristics exist simultaneously within the same substance in the present."
According to the explanation of the meaning, the characteristic of cessation is past.
A question is raised:
If that were so, it would contradict the scriptural statement that "there is birth, aging, and cessation simultaneously."
The commentary states:
It is not necessarily the case that four characteristics occurring simultaneously is what is meant by "immediacy" (*jī*).
What is now referred to as "establishing" (*lì*) is as follows:
That which is the very dharma arising is precisely that which shall perish; there is no other separate dharma.
Therefore, it is called "identical" (*jī*). Ce says:
Describing two interpretations from the West:
the first states that the three characteristics have no sequence of before and after.

Therefore, when the characteristic of arising (*jāti*) of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) occurs, it is at the very moment the dharma ceases; it is not said that two dharmas manifest simultaneously.
One view holds that the three characteristics—namely, arising (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), and change (*anyathātva*)—exist sequentially.

The characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) exist simultaneously. Therefore, for a given dharma, the characteristic of abiding and the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) may both coexist in the present world,
because these three characteristics are all within a single moment of the present.
The fourth characteristic, cessation, exists in the past;
therefore, it is said that "each and every moment" and so forth.
Within this very context, it refers to the point up until one correctly contemplates [the dharma] as ceasing.
The new and old dependently originated states are not the same as the previous formations;
now, birth is further explained. Ji says:
If that which is presently existing were called "ceasing" at the same time as its alteration,
then cessation would be a non-existent entity (abhāva), whereas duration and alteration would be existent entities (bhāva).
How can there be both existence and non-existence at the same time?
Therefore, this treatise states:
"From these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), after the moment [of their arising]..."
The very momentary destruction of the intrinsic nature of these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen is precisely what is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
It is by virtue of the existence of a phenomenon that, at no [other] time, it reaches the past that the characteristic of cessation is established.
Therefore, arising and ceasing, as well as light and darkness, do not exist simultaneously.
[The opponent] asks:
If this is so, then a single kṣaṇa would lack the four characteristics.
The commentary states:
When this phenomenon ceases and that phenomenon arises,
it is like the two ends of a scale reaching equilibrium.
Therefore, in a single moment there is both arising and ceasing.
If this is so, why does the doubt not arise as to whether ceasing occurs first and arising later?
The explanation is as follows:
Since it was stated from the outset that there must be arising at the initial moment, a question is asked:
In the various sūtras, it is said that there are three conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*). What are these three?
The commentary states:
There are two meanings.
First, the inclusion, abiding, entry, and differentiation.
Because it abides in a semblance of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, if one hears that all phenomena have abiding, the mind will become weary of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and lack vigor.
Moreover, abiding can draw forth subsequent births of phenomena, rendering it ineffective in their cessation.
Therefore, grasping (saṃgraha), abiding (sthiti),
and entering (praveśa) are distinct; the two [other] theories hold that grasping,
abiding, and entering are distinct because abiding possesses functional efficacy within its own moment.
That which has arisen but not yet perished is called "abiding.
Therefore, there exists a functional capacity distinct from the aforementioned dharma;
it has no efficacy with respect to its own mindfulness.
Therefore, "arising" (*utpāda*) is included within "entry" (*praveśa*).

Furthermore, because it is distinct from and conforms to the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), "arising" is included within "entry. If this is so, why is "arising" not also included within "cessation"?
The commentary says:
"Difference" refers to existence (bhāva), while "extinction" refers to non-extinction (aniruddha).
One is of the past, and the other is of the present.
Although their characteristics may appear similar, they cannot be subsumed under the characteristic of cessation.
Here is another explanation:
although the characteristic of cessation belongs to the past in terms of its temporal stage, it is provisionally established as a characteristic.
Because that which exists in the present is necessarily subject to cessation at the time of its destruction,
this indicates that the subsequent non-existence of this present phenomenon is its characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).
For this reason, a single moment possesses four characteristics.
However, this treatise speaks from the perspective of the state of actual non-existence;
therefore, it says that after the moment [of the third], there is again a fourth.
From here on, the second section extensively refutes the externalist attachments.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
there exists a separate entity for the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) that are neither matter nor mind, distinct from the phenomena themselves;
while these possess separate entities that exist simultaneously, their functions occur sequentially.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the four characteristics do not exist as distinct entities apart from phenomena such as matter and mind at their respective times; therefore,
they are said to be "of the same substance."
However, because [a phenomenon] first arises, next abides, finally changes, and subsequently ceases, it is called "different times. Now,
the Mahāyāna teaches that if the conventional and the real follow divergent paths, [then...]
If one employs different versions, it is said that their characteristics and principles differ;
this is not the same as the *Tattvasiddhi*.
If one investigates the provisional, it is not separate from the real.
By inferring that the effect does not depart from the cause,
it is stated that there are no four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) external to the dharma itself;
this differs from the Sarvāstivāda school.
Furthermore, the three characteristics occur simultaneously;
they do not, like the realization of true reality, occur exclusively at different times,
nor do arising and cessation occur sequentially.
This differs from the Sarvāstivāda position that the four characteristics are always and simultaneously present.
The text is divided into two parts;
the first refutes their substantial existence by means of the two characteristics of "greatness" and "smallness."
Second, from "Furthermore, good son" onwards, [the text] refutes their substantial existence by means of observing them as conventionally existent.
Within the preceding section, there are two parts;
first, a brief refutation of the four characteristics external to dharmas.
Second, regarding these four types [of views], the following extensively refutes the four characteristics held by those outside the Dharma.
Within this, first, prior to the refutation, the correct principle is set forth;
second, from "In this regard, the bodhisattva... onwards, the erroneous attachments are refuted.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that [the aggregates] are not real through general observation;
second, from "Furthermore, all bodhisattvas... onwards, refuting their substantial existence by means of specific reasoning.
In the preceding section, it asks: "For what reason... up to 'there is nothing else that arises, ages, abides, or ceases'?
Ji [Daoshi] asks:
"Why is there such a discrepancy?"
Furthermore, the four characteristics are mentioned again because they encompass both the phenomena to be included and the phenomena to be excluded.
Since the phenomena to be included mutually encompass one another, there are merely the expressions: "conditioned phenomena arise," up to "conditioned phenomena abide, age, and perish."
If a phenomenon is to be negated,
it must be negated by means of its specific four characteristics;
because these phenomena are pervasive, all four characteristics are cited collectively.
Question: Why,
in the refutation of arising, do you not merely speak of "arising," but likewise [refute] even "abiding" and "cessation"?
The commentary says:
Because that which abides also possesses arising;
and because at the time of arising, there is abiding and so forth.
Therefore, "the Great Birth gives rise to the eight dharmas," and so forth;
thus, pervasion is negated.
The second section of the text is divided into two parts.
First, the existence of substantiality is refuted by means of the four characteristics.
Second, regarding the phrase "if the dharma of cessation," the existence of substantiality is specifically refuted by means of the characteristic of cessation.
As for the statement that such investigation yields nothing findable, it refers to the phrase "if one is separated from those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth."
This refutation implies that the arising of the arising of form must also have an arising;
this is precisely what is called "small arising" (*kṣudra-utpāda*) in the Hīnayāna.
If one says they are one, it does not accord with reason.
The arising of the small is inherently one with the arising of the great;
likewise, the arising of the great that produces all conditioned phenomena is one with those very phenomena.
Therefore, to conceive of an arising as distinct [from these] is called a futile exertion.
This leads even to what is illogical.
As for the statement that it is "illogical" if they are different:
if one were to claim that a small birth arises from a great birth despite their essential natures and characteristics being distinct, that would be irrational.
Then it would follow that the "small arising" (anutpāda) is substantially different from the "arising" (utpāda) itself and is capable of producing the essence of arising;
however, since both are equally distinct [from arising], this is not logical.
Master Ji’s commentary states:
"That which is not produced by conditioned activity (saṃskāra) is 'small production';
that which is produced by conditioned activity is 'great production.'"
If you say that the arising of the great and the arising of the small are different,
then the arising of the small should likewise be capable of producing form, just as the arising of the great produces the dharmas of form;
furthermore, the arising of the great should also be able to produce the arising of the small.

If the "small birth" (*parittabhava*) were to give rise to the "great birth" (*mahābhava*), it should likewise give rise to material phenomena (*rūpadharma*). Therefore, the "small birth" is not the "volitional birth" (*saṃskārabhava*) capable of producing material phenomena;
rather, it should be the "great birth" that is the "volitional birth."
Therefore, it is not logical for the two [arising and ceasing] to be distinct.
Below, the characteristic of cessation is refuted individually.

The intention is this: if there were a characteristic of cessation that was distinct from the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and yet caused those conditioned phenomena to cease, [it would be untenable].
In that case, the single characteristic of cessation would cause all phenomena to cease,
because they possess distinct natures yet share the characteristic of cessation;
it is just as when light arises, all darkness is extinguished.
In this way, with little exertion of effort during the night, one can extinguish all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*),
just as when entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), where all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) are entirely extinguished.
Furthermore, since previously conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) ceased due to the arising of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*),
those very conditioned phenomena should arise again once they have ceased by means of that same characteristic of cessation;
for there would be no factor to oppose them.
Master Ji said:
"To judge this passage as the second distinct refutation of the characteristic of cessation is incorrect.
If one understands that 'the arising of that arising' serves as an analogy for the other characteristics, then the subsequent refutation of cessation is raised below."
In sum, it is thus. Regarding the second point, the contemplation of conventional existence (*prajñaptisat*) is established to refute substantial existence (*dravyasat*).

That is to say: furthermore, if a son of good family contemplates that the phenomena of the three periods of time, though substantially existent, are merely conventional, and thereby attains liberation.
This is not logical; this is the refutation.
That which is contrary to this is what is logical.
Because one understands that phenomena of the three times are provisional by means of their provisionality, one attains liberation.
In the explanation of selflessness, it says:
"To fully know the nature of the two kinds of selflessness of all phenomena."
The *Purāṇa-śāstra* states:
"Regarding all phenomena, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no self (*ātman*) nor what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).
One knows, in accordance with reality, that sentient beings lack a self and that phenomena lack a self."
According to the traditional interpretation,
"non-self" refers to the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*),
while "self and what belongs to self" refers to the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Now it is not so. To say that [the self] is not [identical to] the dharmas implies that the dharmas themselves are also not [the self].
This means that when [the self] is refuted, one realizes that the aggregates (skandhas) are distinct from the imagined self.
In explaining the tranquility of nirvāṇa,
there is first the teaching and then the analogy.
Within the teaching, the name "nirvāṇa" is explained first.
Next, the essence of *nirvāṇa* is presented;
this will later be analyzed in terms of persons.
As for the statement, "the prior causes are eternally severed":
This is cessation with remainder;
that which is subsequent cessation without remainder is cessation without remainder.
Regarding the statement that "the remainder ultimately does not arise or originate" is called *nirvāṇa*:
because the afflictions, karma, and suffering that would otherwise arise from the causes and conditions of birth and death no longer arise at all, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, the permanent abandonment of prior causes occurs in the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga),
while the subsequent cessation without remainder occurs in the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
Moreover, the prior permanent abandonment of causes occurs through the suppression of the active afflictions during the stage of preparatory application (prayoga).
Later, when the seeds are extinguished through cessation without remainder,
that which remains will never arise again;
this refers to the non-arising of the fruit.
Because it severs the cause,
the essential nature [of the path] is next presented.
Below, this is distinguished according to the [four] entrances.
Bodhisattvas prior to the stages have not yet seen the śrāvakas;
although they verbally describe nirvāṇa as quiescent,
they have not yet been able to realize it through direct realization.
He is also capable of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*),
meaning he possesses the mental attention that reflects upon the teachings.
Below, a simile is explained.
First, the analogy of the prince is presented;
next, the analogy of the sick person is presented.
Within the former, the illustration precedes the application.
There are three analogies here:
first, the analogy of taking the false for the true;
second, the analogy of hearing the truth but not yet understanding it.
Regarding the third analogy on the true shame of awakening,
concerning the mention of "deer, oxen, horses, and elephants," there is an interpretation as follows:
The deer dwelling in the mountain thickets is used as a metaphor for the pratyekabuddha.
The ox being slow and the horse being swift are metaphors for those śrāvakas who are dull-witted or sharp-witted, respectively.
The elephant is a metaphor for the bodhisattva.
Master Ji said: "This metaphor illustrates the four types of nirvana;
the elephant symbolizes non-abiding nirvana."
The remaining three lack a guide, which we shall not now evaluate according to their meaning.
That is to say, the deer, dwelling constantly in the stillness of the mountains from beginning to end, is a metaphor for primordial purity.
The ox, because it has horns, is a metaphor for having a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
Because a horse has no horns, it serves as a metaphor for the absence of the remainder of dependence (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
Within the application (*yojana*), there are again three [points].
In the third application, when the noble ones of the three vehicles enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they realize the principle of *tathatā*.
This is precisely what is called the "wisdom of direct realization regarding true nirvāṇa.
The second analogy of the sick person clarifies that the teaching must correspond to the capacity of the recipient. The preceding is the analogy;
the following is the application.
There are six analogies:
first, the analogy of responding to the stimulus of a disciple to manifest a sage;
second, the analogy of hearing the teaching and transforming one's attachments.
Third is the analogy of encouraging one to hear the supreme Dharma;
fourth is the analogy of not relinquishing prior attachments;
fifth is the analogy of explaining the varying depths of the teachings.
Sixth, the fool who does not understand the parable.
This section has three parts;
first, the application of the preceding fifth parable.
This may also be understood as subsuming the preceding five similes;
next, it subsumes the sixth simile.
This is subsequently done in order to distinguish pure faith.
Regarding the statement "if it is superior and most superior, even up to and including the most excellent," Jing says:
"As for the first three phrases..."
The latter is called the "Correct Teaching.
The first teaching is called "Superior," and the subsequent teaching is called "Superior and Victorious."
The final stage is called the ultimate limit.
Regarding the subsequent three phrases:
"lower" refers to providing instruction so as to cause [the practitioner] to initiate practice.
There are inferior, middling, and superior [levels] corresponding to these three phrases.
Regarding the latter three phrases:
the "inferior" refers to providing instruction and admonition to cause one to abandon faults.
There are three types of faults;
these correspond respectively to the three phrases: inferior, middling, and superior.
The "teaching of the Dharma" is the general category.
The latter three phrases are distinct. Tai says:
"The first three phrases explain the three grades of the Bodhisattva Vehicle."
This refers to the three paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.
The next three phrases explain the three grades of the path for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
and the final three phrases explain the three grades of the path for the Śrāvaka.
Furthermore, the first [category] consists of the superior-middle divided into three grades;
the next consists of the middle-middle divided into three grades;
and the last consists of the inferior-middle divided into three grades.
Regarding the "Dharma-teaching" and the "Correct Teaching":
the teaching of skillful means is called the Dharma-teaching,
while the fundamental teaching is called the Correct Teaching.
Ji said: "The first set of three phrases, beginning with 'supremely [vast],' refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
The second set of three phrases, beginning with 'profoundly [vast],' refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*)."

The three phrases beginning with "supreme" (*parama*) refer to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because within each of the three types of wisdom there are superior, middling, and inferior levels.
Furthermore, the "Dharma-teaching" (*dharmadeśanā*) and "correct teaching" (*samyag-deśanā*) refer to these three grades of phrases: superior, middling, and inferior.
The three phrases beginning with "profound" (*gambhīra*) constitute the three grades of instruction (*śāsana*);
the three phrases beginning with "supreme" (*viśiṣṭa*) constitute the three grades of admonition (*avavāda*).

Furthermore, within each of the three types of wisdom mentioned previously, these three phrases—namely, the teaching of the Dharma (*dharma-śāsana*), the correct teaching (*samyak-śāsana*), and so forth—are to be applied in successive order.
Chapter on Merit (11b). Regarding the Chapter on Merit: the preceding section clarifies the capacity for training through ten chapters, which are divided into three parts.
The first seven chapters clarify the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāga*).
The preceding two chapters have completed the explanation of superior progress;
now, this chapter explains the fulfillment of the fruit through its causes.
"Merit" (gong) refers to labor or achievement.
"Virtue" (guǎngdé) refers to the Way and its power (dàodé).
To attain this virtue through the application of effort is called "merit" (gōngdé).
This section provides a detailed explanation of it, hence it is titled the "Chapter on Merit."
In this passage, there is first the question and then the explanation.
Five verses clarify twenty-seven types of dharma-gates;
twenty-five of these specifically elucidate the qualities of merit.
From this point on, they are designated by name;
though appearing similar to virtues, they are in reality not virtues,
as they arise merely because they accompany [the primary marks].
The five verses are divided into four sections;
since the final two verses constitute one section,
the first verse enumerates seven names.
The prose section provides a sequential explanation.
Regarding the statement that "a bodhisattva who accomplishes five kinds of non-marvelous dharmas is said to accomplish most marvelous dharmas," Jing says:
To benefit others as if it were one's own business is not considered extraordinary; however,
when one investigates its root, there is no basis for it other than the Great Compassion that embraces others as oneself— therefore,
know this to be truly extraordinary.
Ji said: "Judging by the signs,
everyone is capable of receiving it."
This is not extraordinary.
If we discuss it from the perspective of the mind,
undertaking such a task without hesitation is what is called an extraordinary phenomenon.
Furthermore, it is not particularly remarkable when compared with its own kind;
however, it is most extraordinary when compared with the two vehicles.
As for those who remain silent and find no flavor [in this teaching]:
This refers to remaining silent and without speech.
Silence is indeed the flavor of true bliss;
yet, for the sake of sentient beings, one preaches the True Dharma.
Furthermore, having entered nirvāṇa myself,
this silence is indeed the flavor of bliss; yet,
for the sake of sentient beings, I preach the True Dharma.
Ce says: Because vitarka and vicāra give rise to various forms of verbal expression,
and because from the second dhyāna upward one is free from those causes for giving rise to verbal expression— namely vitarka and vicāra— it is called the flavor of the bliss of silence.
Furthermore, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he relinquishes all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) to take birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in order to benefit them.
One should understand the characteristics of how he performs unfailing application (*avandhya-prayoga*) toward sentient beings through five causes and conditions.
This refers to what was explained previously in the Chapter on Offerings (*pūjā-varga*).
If bodhisattvas possess five characteristics, they can unfailingly perform the deeds of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
First, they first desire to bring about the benefit and happiness of others.
Second, they possess non-erroneous awareness that correctly understands the benefit and happiness of those beings.

Thus, the three types—armor-like diligence (*saṃnāha-vīrya*) and so forth—are assigned to it in sequence.
The nature of giving that is vast and untainted is called "the wisdom of the outstretched hand" (*hasta-prasāra-prajñā-dāna*).
This is also as explained extensively in the previous nine gates concerning generosity.
Regarding the phrase "the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the unerring application of knowledge for their correct induction":
the four analytical knowledges are precisely the nature of wisdom that is capable of understanding profound meanings.
Thus, the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) preceding the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is termed "wisdom of application" (*prayoga-jñāna*).
Regarding the "basis for compassion," Jing says:
The objects are explained as the bases (*āśraya*).
That is to say, because one feels compassion toward those who experience the five kinds of suffering and those who commit evil deeds, they are called bases.
Furthermore, there are also five bases for being able to understand profound meanings and intentional terminology (*abhisandhi*).
Regarding the first basis, Jing says:
"As for the statement 'in accordance with the profound according to the sūtras,' it is because the principle of *tathatā* cannot be fathomed by shallow wisdom."
It is called "profound.
Because the sūtra states that the two kinds of emptiness accord with suchness, it is termed "accordance with the profound.
Regarding "the manifestation of the profound":
Through investigation, the two kinds of emptiness appear as suchness.
Regarding "dependent origination characterized by emptiness," the nature of dependence refers to the four conditions.
Dependent origination refers to the twelve links of dependent origination.
Thus, the nature of dependence and the essence of dependent origination are devoid of a fixed nature and the imagined nature;
therefore, they lead to a correspondence with emptiness.
Ce said: Because the Tathāgata’s teachings always rely upon the two truths, they are called "conformable.
Since the principle of the two truths transcends words and is beyond thought, it is further described as "profoundly, profoundly manifest."
That which is called emptiness is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
That which is dependent origination based on conditions is the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Regarding the fourth basis, Zhongji (基) states:
Regarding the meaning of "all perceptions" (*saṃjñā*):
"perception" refers to the designating name,
while "meaning" refers to that which is designated.
Ce says: "The phrase 'to manifest and eliminate the underlying intentions and so forth' means that one can manifest the esoteric intent to remove the doubts of others."
Regarding the phrase "concerning all dharmas" in the fifth locus,
it refers to the teachings of the Three Piṭakas. "Dharma" here denotes the objective sphere of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
"Meaning" (artha) is the objective sphere of unimpededness regarding meaning;
"etymology" (nirukti) is the objective sphere of unimpededness regarding words;
and "categories" (prabheda) is the objective sphere of unimpededness regarding distinctions.
Regarding the benefits of the fruit of compassion:
first, the benefits of the fruit are explained;
second, scriptural citations are adduced to establish them.
This concludes the subsequent section.
Within the preceding middle section, the first part clarifies self-benefit through the severing of enmity and harm;
the second part, "universally [benefiting] those below," clarifies the benefit of others.

In the *Zhongce* (Commentary on the *Madhyāntavibhāga*), it is stated in the section on citing scriptural authority for proof: "As it is said in the sūtras, there are eleven kinds of benefits from cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*):
one sleeps in peace and awakens in peace."
Protected by the devas and beloved by non-humans,
they will not be harmed by poison or weapons,
nor shall they perish by water or fire.
One will have no bad dreams while sleeping;
after death, one will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven;
and whatever benefit one seeks shall be attained.
Consulting the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*,
and furthermore, the *Vimuktimārga-śāstra* clarifies that there are eleven merits in cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
First, one sleeps peacefully without fear or alarm.
Second, one awakens peacefully without inauspicious signs;
third, one has no evil dreams;
fourth, one is cherished and remembered by others.
Fifth, they are beloved by non-human beings.
Sixth, they are protected by the devas.
Seventh, fire, poison, swords, and staves do not affect their bodies.
Eighth, one quickly attains meditative concentration;
ninth, the complexion of the face is radiant;
tenth, at the time of death, the mind is not disturbed.
Eleventh: those who have not yet attained the supreme Dharma are born in the Brahma Heaven.
*Bunpin* (Section on Divisions). *Bunpin*: the sound of Brahma (*bun*) is like a thin blade (*bin*); this term contains three meanings.
First, the meaning of stages;
second, the meaning of the differentiation of categories;
third, the meaning of wings.
The former title, "Chapter on Wings," means that by practicing four dharmas, one can swiftly attain the fruit;
it is like a bird relying on its wings to reach its destination quickly.
Now, following those two categories of bodhisattvas—those who remain at home and those who have gone forth—I shall establish the titles for the respective chapters.
The basis for the five characteristics does not depart from these two categories of householders and renunciants.
Therefore, following the "Chapter on Mutual Causality," the next section discusses the "Chapter on Analysis.
Within this text, first the topical outline is presented;
second, the four chapters are explained in their proper sequence.
Third, the general analysis.
Regarding the statement in the *Exposition of Skillful Means* (*Upāyakauśalya-vyākhyāna*), "As previously [stated],
so it is here in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*," the former four are as explained in the twelve skillful means.
The fifth is as in the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic);
the sixth is as in the *Vinaya* (Precepts);
the seventh is as in the five vows.
The latter three textual passages are not uniform;
they are found, for instance, as explained in the *Bodhipakṣa-paṭala*.
Regarding the phrase "according to their lineage, faculties, and so forth":
The Tripitaka Master says:
"Seeds" refers to the name and clan;
"active manifestation" refers to the faculties.
Regarding the passage in the *Vyākhyāyukti* stating, "It can provide benefit to some sentient beings, up to and including a portion of happiness and a portion of both," Wonch'uk says:
"Thus, each of these four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) possesses both benefit and happiness."
Furthermore, although one bestows wealth upon others, causing them to generate the resolve [for awakening] and so forth, this constitutes benefit (*hitā*).
To obtain the use of material goods in the present constitutes happiness (*sukha*), and so forth.
In this manner, each and every [aspect] is fully possessed.
It should be understood accordingly. If it were not so,
then beneficial conduct and pleasant speech would be taught as increasing [the benefit].
Generosity is [the means of] bringing peace and happiness;
acting in concert with others applies to both [wholesome and unwholesome deeds], because one acts in concert with them in both good and evil.
Regarding the three gates within non-erroneous dedication:
first, the thorough cultivation of activities;
second, skillful means.
Third, benefiting others.
Within the general analysis, there are two parts.
First, it is clarified that these four [categories] universally encompass all the trainings for both householders and renunciants.
Second, it is explained that although householders and renunciants alike practice the four matters, there is a great disparity in their relative excellence.
It is the renunciant bodhisattva who is able to practice the "linked chain" (*śṛṅkhalā*) of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Jizang said: "The meaning of 'hook and chain' (gou-so) is to take the sense of mutual restriction and obstruction.
For those who have left the household life, there are prohibitions and restraints intended to prevent the three types of unwholesome karma."
Therefore, it is like a chain of hooks;
a bodhisattva living at home is not like this.

*Chapter on Superior Intention* (11b). In this chapter, it is explained in detail that among the intentions of bodhisattvas who have entered the generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), there are seven types of intention for the benefit of others and fifteen types for both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
The title is derived from this.
The preceding "Chapter on Characteristics" and the division of chapters both concern the practice of cultivation.
The practices that arise must necessarily be generated from one's underlying intention (*āśaya*).
Therefore, following the classification of the chapters, the next section clarifies the mental disposition (*āśaya*).
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
desire (*chanda*) and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) constitute the essence of the mental disposition.
Regarding the *Vyākhyāyukti*,
[it states that] aspiration (*chanda*) and volition (*cetanā*) constitute the nature of the intention (*āśaya*). Kīrti says:
In this context, although the term "predominant" (*adhipati*) appears to apply only to the [form] realm,
there is no contradiction in taking it as applicable to the stage prior to that (the desire realm) as well, based on the meaning derived from the text.
Within the text, the question is posed first and the answer follows later.
In the response, the first verse sets forth the topical outline (*uddāna*),
while the subsequent prose commentary explains according to those topics. Within the verse,
the first half generally enumerates the seven aspects of benefiting others.
Regarding "compassion," the latter half [of the verse] summarizes fifteen types of intention and activity.
This is explained in the prose commentary in two parts:
first, the explanation of compassion, and second, the explanation of intention.
Regarding the statement in the preceding section that "one is called 'possessing a benevolent intention' because one is endowed with compassion," Jing says:
"It should be understood that the seven kinds of compassion are merely conceptualizations of loving-kindness and compassion."
Compassion is devoid of the nature of malice;
its essence consists of true compassion and wisdom.
Furthermore, these seven types may also be considered aspects of the underlying intention (*āśaya*).
It is called "compassion" (anukampā) because it is associated with compassion.
Beiyun states:
"Adhimokṣa and adveṣa are both termed 'compassion' by virtue of their attendant factors."
In its essential nature, it is still resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Furthermore, it is explained that the name used in the sūtras and śāstras is not fixed.
Some say that wisdom is called great compassion;
it is the contemplation of things as they truly are,
which may occur in the present life.
Regarding the statement "in the contemplation of the immeasurable joy of conceptualization,

one never employs what is not the Dharma," this means that one does not exhort or instruct sentient beings by means of the ten non-virtues, what is not the Dharma, what is not the Vinaya, improper conduct of the wise, the false teachings of external paths, or irrational positions.
Regarding the statement, "This is called 'unstained' (arāga) and also called 'objectless' (anālambana)," Wonhyo’s commentary explains:
"To not pray for blessings is called 'unstained.'"
Not praying for future results is called "without conditions" (*anaimittika*).
Furthermore, both types are termed "untainted" (*asaṃkliṣṭa*);
"tainted" refers to both present afflictions and the fruits of future worlds.
Therefore, the conditions (pratyaya) are also applied to this.
The second explanation, concerning the fifteen types of intention (āśaya), is divided into four parts.
First, the essence is analyzed and the names are listed.
The second is the explanation;
the third clarifies how the fifteen intentions can perform ten functions;
and the fourth is the summary that clarifies their sharpness.
Among these fifteen, the first seven are named after their objects;
the next three are named after their meanings;
and the final five receive their designations according to their positions.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, the impure intention (*āśaya*) of bodhisattvas is what is called the 'intention to be disciplined' (*vinayitavya-āśaya') and so forth":

this refers to those prior to the [bodhisattva] grounds who have not yet realized the Dharma, but are instead disciplined through the four means such as manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and so on.
From the eighth stage onward, having realized *tathatā* through self-realization and having cultivated it for many eons, supernormal powers arise simultaneously with the body;
therefore, the pure and thoroughly pure intention is the "simultaneously arisen intention."
Because it is established as thoroughly purified through the nature of pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*).
Regarding the section on "Abiding" (Chapter 11b): what is the meaning of "abiding"?
It is called "abiding" because within the twelve stages of a bodhisattva's abidings—both conditioned and unconditioned—one is able to abide.
Because this section explains these matters in detail, it is called the "Chapter on Abiding.
Previously, the various practices of the bodhisattva assembly were not explained in detail;
yet practice must necessarily rely upon stages.
Therefore, following the Chapter on Aspiration (Adhimukti), the Chapter on Abiding (Vihāra) is now elucidated.
Within this chapter, first the preceding inquiry is restated,
followed by the citation of the number and the enumeration of the names.
The subsequent section consists of questions and answers providing an explanation.
Within the preceding [section], there are three phrases. The first restates what was previously mentioned.
Second is the enumeration following the birth;
third is the listing of names.

Thus, beginning from the full possession of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), it is explained at length up to the bodhisattva who practices with right diligence in accordance with what has been taught regarding the bodhisattva’s training.
This summarizes the eighteen chapters within the first *dhāraṇī*:
from the initial "Lineage" chapter up to the "Qualities" chapter.
Regarding the phrase "the various characteristics of bodhisattvas as described appear correctly and equally":
This is called the "Chapter on the First Characteristic" within this *Dhāraṇī*.
It is the section concerning those who train with right diligence in the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) pertaining to the various stages of a bodhisattva.
Regarding the "aspirations of bodhisattvas" as they have been described,
this refers to the section on aspirations;
it enumerates the various qualities of the assembly of bodhisattvas after their descent [into the world].
Within this, first the bodhisattva abodes are presented,
followed by the Tathāgata abodes.
Among the enumeration of their names, the first two verses are presented.
The second prose section corresponds [to the following]:
regarding the three abodes of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), it says, "That is to say, the bodhisattvas truly understand that which can exhort toward reality, etc.
This means that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are the means of observation.
In the fourth stage, one contemplates that which contemplates;
the factors of the path and the various truths are what is contemplated.
In the fifth stage, one contemplates that which is contemplated.
The Bodhisattva of the sixth stage observes and knows that sentient beings undergo the flow of manifold sufferings due to delusion and lack of wisdom,
whereas their manifold sufferings cease through awakening and the possession of wisdom.
In the seventh stage, the continuity of true contemplation is called "uninterrupted.
Although it also takes conventional reality as its object, because one dwells predominantly in *tathatā* (suchness), it is called the "dwelling in the signless" (*animittavihāra*). Ji says:
It is not that there is no intervening tainted mind;
rather, because the discourse concerns a continuous succession of predominantly untainted contemplations,
it is said to be "uninterrupted," though it is not actually uninterrupted.
In the eighth stage, the simultaneous contemplation of the ultimate and the conventional is called "uninterrupted.
Because one proceeds from the contemplation of the ultimate, it is named the "Abode of Signlessness" (*animittavihāra*).
The *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* states:
Because one does not perceive the marks of either awakening or sentient beings, it is called "signless.
In the second question-and-answer explanation, there is first a brief summary and then a detailed exposition.
Within the brief summary, there are two parts.
First, there is the individual explanation;
second, the general analysis.
Regarding the dwelling of the spiritual lineage (*gotrastha*), the question "What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the spiritual lineage? asks about the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the lineage.
Regarding the question, "How does a bodhisattva abide in the lineage-abiding?"— which asks about the person capable of abiding—
the response answers the two preceding questions comprehensively by means of three points.
First, it concerns the cultivation of innate merit and virtue.
Second, it clarifies that they have already possessed the seeds of the Buddha-dharma;
third, it clarifies that their nature is free from coarse defilements such as the immediate karmic offenses (*ānantarya-karma*).
Regarding the former, Jing says:

This means that for bodhisattvas dwelling in the nature of the lineage (*gotra*), from their natural benevolence and maturity up to their possession of numerous wholesome qualities, these constitute the seed;
and these also manifest in their active engagement (*samudācāra*).
Prior to the ten stages of faith, one remains in the state of transmigration;
by the power of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
such a practitioner frequently gives rise to merit-constituting virtues (*puṇyabhāgīya-kuśala*) rather than liberation-constituting virtues (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśala*).
If one gives rise to the wholesome roots conducive to liberation, this constitutes the stage of the ten faiths;
these ten faiths are subsumed within the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*),
and not within the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*).
The subsequent section clarifies the remaining stages of practice:
from the initial generation of the mind of awakening until one has not yet attained pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*),
all practices whatsoever constitute the stage of dwelling in conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).
Thus, one should know that all the various virtues arising while abiding in the lineage (gotra) are undoubtedly portions of merit.
As for the statement that "by virtue of an inherently benevolent and noble nature, one is impelled toward skillful means, rather than through deliberate deliberation," it means:
Driven by the power of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), they cultivate the wholesome factors conducive to merit and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "the many wholesome dharmas appropriate for a bodhisattva manifest therein," there are two interpretations.
The initial text states:
Prior to the ten stages (bhūmi), a bodhisattva is said to "dwell in the lineage" (gotrastha);
this refers to the period before the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Regarding those roots of merit conducive to merit that ought to be manifested in practice, there is the sense that they can indeed be manifested in dependence upon them;
however, once [the bodhicitta] has been generated, they are no longer manifested.
A second [master] says:
The Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are also called "lineage" (*gotra*).
Regarding those dharmas that are to be cultivated as wholesome,
these are the six *pāramitās* with outflows (*sāsrava*).
If one follows the former interpretation,
it differs slightly from the *Saṃgrahaṇī*.
The *Saṃgrahaṇī* divides the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas into three stages and five persons.
Based on these three stages, five types of persons constitute the twelve abodes.
That "abiding in the lineage" (*gotrastha*) refers to the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*);
however, what is here termed "lineage" refers to the state prior to the arousal of that thought, and thus the two do not correspond.
The Tripitaka Master examined the Sanskrit original of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and found that the passage concerning the twelve stages (*dvādaśa-vihāra*) is now absent; therefore,
there is no need for further reconciliation or interpretation.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is also a text that abides by the literal wording;
it is verified as erroneous that the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated it thus:
"It maintains all seeds of the Buddha-dharma within its internal essence. This [correct version] states: "It abides and sustains all seeds of the Buddha-dharma within its internal essence."
Jingyun: This statement is a general summary.
Regarding the phrase "already fully present within the basis":
This refers specifically to the individual case;
thus, within the ālayavijñāna, that which maintains those seeds is called the "basis" (*āśraya*).
Cè states: [as follows].

This is identical in meaning to what was explained above regarding the excellence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) within the lineage (*gotra*), which continues in succession from beginningless time as a natural law (*dharmatā*).
Within its own essence and within its basis, it is still the *ālayavijñāna* as described in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
There are two bases for the seeds:
first, according to the perspective of ultimate reality, they depend upon the ālayavijñāna;
second, according to the perspective of conventional functioning, they abide within the body of the five aggregates.
Next, it says: "From Bodhisattvas whose nature is detached, even down to those who commit the acts of immediate retribution. Jing says:
"Although Bodhisattvas of the spiritual lineage (gotra) may still circulate among the ranks of ordinary beings,"
It is not the case that one who gives rise to fierce and coarse anger, commits the five deeds of immediate retribution, holds wrong views that sever the roots of goodness, or—
as in the cases of King Ajātaśatru killing his father or Devadatta shedding the blood of the Buddha— [is necessarily destined for hell].

These were all long-practicing bodhisattvas who manifested in the form of ordinary people as a skillful means to guide and receive those who have committed the five heinous crimes, causing them to repent and reform. Tai said:
There are two types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*). First is the natural lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*),
which refers to those ordinary beings who, from beginningless time, possess the Mahāyāna lineage and yet commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) and sever the roots of goodness.
Second is the lineage of cultivation (*śikṣāgotra*),
which refers to the generation of the bodhicitta prior to the ten stages of faith as well as during the ten stages of faith itself. Here,
the lineage of cultivation is being elucidated.
Therefore, their nature is free from coarse defilements.

Within the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā*), it is stated that "from the initial generation of the mind up until it is called the stage of practice through conviction" (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*);
this specifies the scope of that stage of practice.
Ce says: He provides two interpretations.
The first says:
Those from the stage of the Ten Faiths upward are all called the Abiding of Arising the Mind.
One school of thought maintains that only from the Ten Understandings upward is one said to have "arisen the mind."

Regarding the statement that within the stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotrastha*), there is only the transformation of the cause (*hetu-parāvṛtti*) which encompasses those causes for the other eleven stages as well as the stage of the Tathāgata:
this distinguishes the differences by contrasting the preceding and succeeding stages.
This means that while abiding in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), one only establishes the causes for subsequent stages;
the actual practice of setting out toward them has not yet arisen as manifest activity. Jing says:
This shows that among the previously explained stages of the lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), one manifests various practices;
it should be understood that this manifestation consists solely of the meritorious portion, which is attained all at once and purified all at once. Master Yuan says:
The various stages (*vihāra*) of a bodhisattva are attained and purified gradually;
only the stage of the Tathāgata is attained and purified instantaneously.
It is called "instantaneous attainment" because the practice of the teaching is perfected all at once.
Because the practice of realization is manifested all at once, it is called "sudden purification.
Why then say that those bodhisattvas abide [in this stage]?
Because there are immeasurable categories of specific objects to be remedied within their respective abidings.
Because the Tathāgata’s dwelling has only one grade of obstruction,
there is this distinction. Master Ce says:
Regarding the attainment of all merits, why would they be attained all at once?
Regarding the abandonment of all faults, why would they be purified all at once?
If one considers their actual manifestation, they cannot be practiced simultaneously.
However, because they are matured, it is said that they are attained instantaneously.

Within the section on dwelling in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), it says: "One is able [to exercise] the various gateways regarding all phenomena—namely, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). These are the four analytical powers (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
The detailed analysis within the intermediate section is concluded.
From here on, there are two general clarifications:
first, explaining the differences in their functions.
Second, it clarifies the distinctions regarding the attainment of the signless (*animitta*) among those at the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā*) and others.

The reason the "abiding in the spiritual lineage" (*gotra-vihāra*) is not mentioned here is that this section intends only to distinguish the characteristics of the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) and the commencement of practice.
Since these characteristics do not exist at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), they are not further explained here.
As for the limited scope of the activities performed during the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*):
Master Yuan said: "Because the inclination and practice are limited to a small scope, it is called 'narrow';
because one cannot practice constantly, it is called 'deficient.'"
Because the functioning mind is not virtuous, it possesses indetermination;
because it loses [its state] upon encountering conditions, it possesses regression. Jing said:
The various practices that have been initiated have not yet realized the *dharmadhātu*; their scope of activity remains narrow and limited.
They have not yet abandoned faults and remain deficient;
because these practices may arise or not arise, they are termed "indeterminate."
The stage prior to the bhūmis is the position of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
which possesses all forms of regression.
In the six stages beginning with the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā*), practice is termed "vast" because it accords with the *dharmadhātu*.
Free from faults and endowed with no deficiency,
constantly initiating all practices is called "certainty. Realizing the principle and being endowed with non-retrogression— this is the perfection of certainty.
The seventh stage possesses the first signlessness;
the eighth stage possesses the second signlessness.
From the seventh stage downward, one gives rise to all practices within each individual practice.
Because all practices are initiated within all practices from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they are "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
The final limit of effort in the seventh stage is adjacent to the eighth stage;
for this reason, it is collectively designated as "immeasurable."
Master Ji said:
"The fact that there is regression in what has been attained reveals that practice is not fixed.
Furthermore, that which is not fixed means that one's actions are not pure."
Those who regress cannot advance purely;
furthermore, those who are not settled still harbor hesitation.
Because those who regress cannot achieve further progress, they fall back.
Within the differentiation of the absence of marks,
according to the older treatises,
there are only four propositions.
Because one dwells in the two signless states and practices the cultivation of purity in their integration,
this treatise presents five points.
First, prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), although one is unable to correctly abide in signless *tathatā*, there is nevertheless the initial setting forth toward it.
Second, because the six preceding stages, although practiced within the dwelling of signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*), have not yet reached perfection, they are described as "narrowly attained.
Third, regarding the seventh stage, which possesses complete realization, there are two interpretations concerning its distance from this [state].
One interpretation states:
the first three stages are identical to those of ordinary beings; in the fourth stage, one practices the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*).
In the fifth stage, there are the four truths.
In the sixth stage, one contemplates dependent origination according to its specific phenomena;

because the contemplation of signlessness is not yet complete, it is not called "perfection. In the seventh stage, one relinquishes the various signs of the preceding six stages and enters the ten kinds of sublime practices of the seventh stage; therefore, it is said that signlessness is perfected.
As will be explained in detail later.
One interpretation states: this is explained from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

In the preceding six stages, when entering true contemplation (*tattva-darśana*), it is brief and when arising in conventional contemplation (*saṃvṛti-darśana*), it is frequent; thus they are not called "perfect.
In the seventh stage, because one enters true contemplation frequently and emerges from it infrequently, it is said to be "perfect."
Furthermore, on this stage, because one practices both the ultimate and the conventional truths simultaneously, it is called "perfection.
Fourth, the eighth stage possesses purity and is free from effort.
Fifth, the ninth and tenth stages possess the fruition of cultivation; because the practice has been fulfilled, they are able only to receive [the results].
Master Jing said:
"From the latter two stages onward, both the ultimate and the conventional are without effortful application;
this is the cultivation and study of signlessness."
From here below is the second [section], which provides an extensive explanation.
Within this, there are also two parts:
first the specific, and later the general.
Regarding the fact that the intention of the first dwelling was not explained previously,
the meaning is as interpreted before. Within the explanation of the dwelling of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), there are two types.
First, the characteristics of conduct are distinguished, followed by the determination of the three grades of patience (*kṣānti*).

Within the former, there is an inquiry regarding the resolution of the knots. As for what constitutes conduct, characteristics, and marks: [the text asks: "What is the conduct? What are the characteristics? What are the marks?"
The Tripiṭaka Master said:
"Activity is the manifestation;
the manifestation is the characteristic."
The names differ, but the meaning is one.

*Nayuta* corresponds here to the number "million" (*jing*).
In the parable, the master craftsman represents the bodhisattva of pure intention.
The fire is a metaphor for the three conditions;
the gold is a metaphor for faith and so forth;
the seventh clarifies the taking of birth.
When those fruits of retribution are categorized,
they are divided into two sections:
first, those that comprise the fruits for householders.
Second, if they delight in initiating the fruit of renunciation that subsumes the lower [levels],
this bodhisattva, dwelling in this stage, frequently becomes an iron-wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who rules over Jambudvīpa and attains great sovereignty.
This is the superior fruit for householders;
it is the complete removal of all stains of stinginess and the like.
This is the most excellent fruit for householders.
Regarding the fruits of renunciation, there are twelve phrases:
first, realizing one hundred samādhis;
second, beholding one hundred Tathāgatas.
Third, they know the transformations and sustaining powers of a hundred Buddhas;
fourth, they can shake a hundred worlds;
fifth, they can abide in a hundred worlds.
Sixth, his light illuminates a hundred worlds;
seventh, he can manifest transformation in a hundred classes of beings;
eighth, he can sustain his life for a hundred kalpas.
Ninth, knowing the events of the past and future limits for a hundred kalpas;
tenth, entering a hundred dharma-gates;
eleventh, manifesting a hundred bodies.
Twelfth, manifesting a hundred retinues within each individual body:
this is the eighth clarity of majestic power,
which corresponds to the fruit of that Buddha’s wisdom.
One should know that what follows below is the third section: the restatement and conclusion.
Above, eight gates were analyzed;
this is the first restatement and conclusion.
